title: Vision Beyond CNNs
summary: Vision Transformers and the self-supervised/multimodal frontier beyond convolutional networks.

slides.subTitle: Treating image patches as tokens
slides.markdown: The **Vision Transformer (ViT)** applies the same Transformer architecture used in NLP to images, by first converting the image into a sequence Transformers can consume: split the image into fixed-size patches (e.g. 16×16 pixels), flatten each patch and linearly project it into an embedding — exactly analogous to a word embedding — then add positional encodings and feed the resulting sequence of "patch tokens" through standard Transformer encoder blocks with self-attention. There is no convolution anywhere in the core architecture; every patch can attend directly to every other patch from the very first layer, which is a fundamentally different inductive bias from how CNNs build up spatial understanding gradually through local receptive fields.

slides.subTitle: CNNs vs ViTs
slides.markdown:
| | CNN | ViT |
|---|---|---|
| Built-in assumption | Nearby pixels are related (locality); the same feature detector works anywhere in the image (translation invariance) | None — must learn spatial relationships purely from data |
| Data efficiency | High — works well on modest datasets | Low — needs very large pretraining datasets to match CNN accuracy |
| Ceiling with abundant data | Strong, but architecture-imposed assumptions can cap it | Higher — no built-in assumptions to eventually outgrow |

CNNs' convolutional filters **bake in** the assumption that local pixel patterns matter and repeat across the image (**inductive bias**) — this is why CNNs work well even with modest data, since the architecture already "knows" something true about images before training starts. ViTs make no such assumption, so they must **learn** spatial structure entirely from data — powerful once there's enough data to learn it from, but a real handicap below that threshold.

slides.subTitle: Training a ViT from scratch on limited data
slides.markdown: A common mistake: choosing a ViT for a project with a modest labeled dataset (a few thousand images) because it's the newer, more powerful-sounding architecture. Trained from scratch at that scale, a ViT typically **underperforms** a comparably-sized CNN, precisely because it lacks the locality/translation-invariance assumptions CNNs get for free — the ViT has to rediscover "nearby pixels tend to be related" purely from limited examples, and often doesn't get there. The fix in practice: either use a CNN for small-data problems, or use a **pretrained** ViT (fine-tuned from a checkpoint trained on hundreds of millions of images) rather than training one from random initialization — the pretraining is what supplies the spatial understanding a small dataset can't.

slides.subTitle: The idea behind contrastive learning
slides.markdown: Labeling millions of images is expensive; **self-supervised pretraining** learns useful visual representations from **unlabeled** images by constructing a proxy task the data itself supplies the answer to. **Contrastive learning** is the dominant approach: create two augmented views of the same image (different crops, color jitter), and train the model so those two views produce **similar** embeddings, while embeddings of views from *different* images are pushed **apart**. No human labels are involved — the "label" is simply "which crops came from the same original image", which is free to generate at any scale. This produces backbones that transfer well to downstream tasks after a much smaller labeled fine-tuning step, similar in spirit to how masked language modeling gives BERT general-purpose representations without labeled text.

slides.subTitle: Bridging vision and language
slides.markdown: Multimodal vision-language models (like CLIP) learn a **shared embedding space** for images and text by training on large sets of (image, caption) pairs, pulling a matching image-caption pair's embeddings close together and pushing mismatched pairs apart — essentially contrastive learning across two modalities instead of two augmented views of one image. Once trained, this shared space enables zero-shot image classification (compare an image's embedding against embeddings of candidate class-name text, no task-specific training needed) and is the backbone technology behind text-to-image generation, covered under [Diffusion Models & Generative AI](diffusion-models-generative-ai).

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: turning an image into patch tokens
slides.markdown:
![A 224x224 image split into a 14x14 grid of 16x16 patches, one patch flattened and linearly projected into an embedding with a position embedding added before entering the Transformer encoder](assets/patch-embedding.svg)

Each patch becomes one token, the same way each word becomes one token in a language Transformer. A 224x224 image split into 16x16 patches yields 196 tokens — small enough for self-attention's quadratic cost to stay tractable, which is why patch size is a real design knob: smaller patches mean more tokens and finer spatial resolution, at higher compute cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: how much data a ViT needs to beat a CNN
slides.markdown:
The original ViT paper's own numbers make the data-hunger concrete: trained only on ImageNet's ~1.3M images, ViT underperformed a comparable ResNet. Trained on JFT-300M (~300M images) before fine-tuning on ImageNet, ViT overtook the CNN. That's roughly a 230x jump in pretraining data needed to flip the result.

This is the practical reason most teams never train a ViT from scratch — they fine-tune a checkpoint someone else already pretrained at that scale, which is exactly the small-dataset pitfall's fix in numbers: the pretraining is buying you what the CNN gets for free from its architecture.

slides.sectionTitle: Masked image modeling: a second self-supervised recipe
slides.subTitle: MAE, alongside contrastive learning
slides.markdown:
**Masked Autoencoders (MAE)** take a different self-supervised route from contrastive learning: mask out a large fraction of an image's patches (75% is typical), feed only the visible patches through the encoder, and train a lightweight decoder to reconstruct the missing pixels. Directly analogous to masked language modeling in BERT, but for images.

The surprisingly high mask ratio matters — images have far more redundancy than text, so a model can only be forced to learn genuine structure (rather than trivially interpolating from nearby visible pixels) if most of the image is hidden. MAE pretraining is cheaper than contrastive learning's paired-view setup and has become a common alternative for pretraining ViT backbones.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming zero-shot CLIP replaces fine-tuning
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "CLIP's zero-shot classification is good enough that fine-tuning a task-specific model is no longer necessary."

**Why it's wrong:** CLIP's zero-shot accuracy is compared against text prompts describing candidate classes, and it degrades on domains far from its web-scale training distribution — fine-grained distinctions (specific bird species, manufacturing defect subtypes) or unusual imaging modalities (satellite, medical) it saw little of during pretraining.

**Correct model:** treat zero-shot multimodal models as a strong, fast baseline and a good fit for open-vocabulary or rapidly-changing label sets — but still fine-tune a task-specific model when the domain is narrow, safety-critical, or measurably underperforms in evaluation against a real labeled sample.
